chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Ja'fari, from Hamdan ibn Ishaq, who said:

I had a son, and gallstones would afflict him. So it was said to me, 'There is no cure for him except that you perform surgery (batth).' So I performed surgery, and he died. So the Shia said, 'You participated in the blood of your son.'

He said, 'So I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Askari (peace be upon him), and he signed: O Ahmad! There is nothing upon you regarding what you did. Rather, you sought the medicine, and his time of death was due to what you did.'

key_terms.الشِّيعَةُ: the Shia (referring to the community or specific group in this context)
key_terms.شَرِكَتَ فِي دَمِهِ: participated in his blood (liability for death)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a father performing surgery on his son if the son dies from the procedure?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'talaqqi al-ajal' (encountering the natural term) in medical procedures, distinguishing between direct causation and incidental death during treatment. Imam al-Askari (peace be upon him) clarifies that since Hamdan’s primary intent was therapeutic rather than fatal, he is exempt from blood money (diya) or culpability, affirming that the son’s death was a result of his destined term coinciding with the surgery. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on intent (niyyah) and the presumption of innocence in medical contexts.
